text: Seven chapters straight assumed you already knew exactly what to build before you started. This one backs up a full step: before you ever drag a single visual onto a canvas, you need to know who's actually looking at this dashboard, what they're trying to decide, and what success even looks like for them.

Four questions, straight from Microsoft's own dashboard design guidance, and genuinely worth memorizing. How does your audience actually use this — checked once a week, or open on a screen all day long? What key metrics actually change what they do next, not just what's technically available to show? What cultural or learned assumptions might shape how they read a color or a layout choice differently than you would? And what do they need in order to succeed — not what happens to be interesting to you, the person building it?

A dashboard sits on top of full reports and semantic models that already hold every last bit of detail. Readers can always drill deeper into a full report from a dashboard tile — so the dashboard itself should show only what someone genuinely needs to monitor at a glance, nothing more. If you catch yourself trying to cram a dozen dimensions onto one page, that detail almost always belongs one click deeper instead.

Write the answers down, even as a handful of quick bullet points — that short brief becomes your reference point for every design decision the rest of this chapter walks through. Next: choosing which KPIs actually earn a spot on the dashboard, and which ones don't.
